item.title: do rationalists care about their health?
item.description:
I always assumed rationalists were health optimizers. I'm not a rationalist, and I kinda assumed that the people who reason carefully about everything would surely reason carefully about what they put in their bodies. And after all, isn't it "rational" to try to live longer, so that you can gain more "utility" from more years of life?

Then I arrived at Lighthaven, where the rationalist community holds its conferences and retreats.

The first thing I noticed were the plastic water bottles everywhere. Did people not mind the microplastics entering their bloodstreams?? And the snacks: kettle chips, Swedish fish, the kind of dried mangoes that have added sugar...

To be clear, I'm not judging. I consume plenty of microplastics and sugary snacks myself. But I was surprised.

To add fuel to the fire, I then heard a rumor that a bunch of rationalists were addicted to nicotine. Isn't that good for your short-term focus, but bad for your long-term health? (To be fair, they were apparently inspired by a post that Gwern wrote, citing a bunch of scientific studies about how nicotine gum isn't actually that bad for you... but still.)

That's when I began to wonder: maybe people consider it rational to take stimulants that boost their short-term mental energy, at the cost of their longevity. Especially if they believe there's a good chance that AI is going to kill us all within the next decade. Maybe under that framework, prioritizing longevity is actually irrational?

So today, I decided to send out a survey on this. I distributed it in the Lighthaven Slack and on Twitter.

Only twenty-nine people have answered thus far, but unfortunately—as I am here for a writing residency and will be kicked out if I don't publish my blog post by tonight—this is all the data we'll have to go off of.

how many respondents were rationalists?

I asked everyone how much they self-identified as a rationalist. Just under half -- 12 out of 29 -- rated themselves 5 or higher out of 7. I will consider those 12 as "rationalists."

do rationalists care about longevity?

I also asked everyone: how much effort do you invest in optimizing your longevity?

The people who scored themselves higher on rationality also reported more effort on longevity.  With a sample this small I expected nothing to hold up, but this one correlation did (Spearman 0.38, p = 0.04) (thanks Claude for the analysis).

are they actually addicted to nicotine?

No. Most people just take caffeine. 4 respondents use nicotine; 6 take a prescription stimulant (e.g. Adderall). There was no significant difference between the rationalist and non-rationalist group.

conclusion

Unfortunately, the survey failed to shed meaningful light on my hypothesis. Maybe I'm totally wrong, or maybe I just need to talk to some more people.

If you are a rationalist and want to share any personal anecdotes on whether it’s rational to care about your longevity, feel free to DM me :)

item.title: The Coziness Problem
item.description:
To spell out this vibe-comic[1]: Safety made the locally correct decision here at every step of a bad situation. But like in Caleb Biddulph's parable, this globally resulted in an awkward state of affairs.

From the Public's POV (penultimate panel), they would naively see AI safety as complicit in the building of the machine. If it really is a doomsday device, why would Safety involve itself at all?

(Safety in turn has a good answer: Public wasn't willing to listen back in the 2010s. Ordinary people would nod along but not lobby their politicians, and politicians would not take it seriously, because most AI experts wouldn't either.)

The realest case of a doomsday device was probably Project Sundial, a bomb so big as to destroy the Earth in one go. When Edward Teller proposed it in backroom briefings, people thought it was an "advertising stunt."

The prior on gadgets truly being doomsday devices is very low. Hence, when even Safety shows some signs of not taking it seriously, the Public doesn't either.

In the final panel, we have Safety looking at the other two characters. In the past, they would be timid about shouting too much to Public, due to Company's implicit threat of bad relations. Company has become more powerful than they were in the 2010s. But in comparison to the now half-sleeping giant, not so much anymore.

I also spent some time researching historical precedents for groups becoming socially cozy with entities they're advocating against:

  • Many of the Manhattan project scientists advocated for treaties, but after they'd already built the A-bomb. Some like Oppenheimer advocated against the H-bomb, and this did not go well. But before the A-bomb most outsiders considered the idea ludicrous (e.g. "That is the biggest fool thing we have ever done. The bomb will never go off, and I speak as an expert in explosives.").
  • Recombinant DNA technology was stopped at Asilomar in 1975, but this was internal to the researchers themselves, without having to involve Public. Safety tried that strategy in 2017, but back then mainstream AI experts were not bought into it. Now that pioneers like Yoshua Bengio and Geoffrey Hinton are on board, the political dynamics have become so warped that they have less voice.
  • There are various examples of environmental groups working closely with the relevant industry for harm reduction. The Environmental Defense Fund is well-known for doing this openly. But environmentalism also has lots of other dysfunctional dynamics which seem to make the circumstances quite different here.

This was a very shallow review, but unfortunately the record is fairly thin, at least in terms of direct analogies.

But we could imagine that General Electric and Ford Motors were doing some large-scale nuclear fission experiments in the 1930s, before almost anyone understood the implications of this. They notice the atmospheric ignition problem, and run some calculations. At some point, they realize they just don't know what will happen, since it comes down to theories they don't yet understand. All the physicists aware of the implications are either working at the labs or closely tied. I don't know what they should do then.

  1. ^

    Artistic disclosure: I hand-drew and scanned the original 10 panels myself, but there's a reason why I literally failed art in high school. It took several iterations of Gemini + Claude to get this, and it's still missing some things.

item.title: Probability, in public communication, is not just "a report of subjective uncertainty"
item.description:
Sometimes the following interaction plays out in public forums:

Lab Employee: I think there is a 20% chance of AI killing us all.

Cope Merchant (Quote Tweet): AI safety people are fearmongering, by pretending they have a hard scientific model, as part of their plan to [unknown]

Rationalist (Quote Tweet): But you see, a probability is just a report of their own epistemic state...

I sympathize with (some of) the words that the cope merchant is saying here. While in our subculture (and possibly Silicon Valley) the report "I think there is a 20% chance that AI kills everyone" means something cousined to "it seems unlikely but far from impossible", that is not all it's conveying to a regular person. To most normies, an ML researcher at a lab sounds like some sort of expert. And an "expert" that states a probability about something within their domain, is not just communicating an opinion on an event's likelihood. There's an implication that the expert arrived at it by some well-understood procedure, because most of the time the probabilities a normie reads are derived in this way (i.e. in rain forecasts, surgery odds, polls.)

This implication affects how most listeners update on the result, and probably does for you in regular life too. For example, if your financial advisor told you that your portfolio had a 0.05% chance of going bust, and then later on claimed that they had just "guessed" and ran no actual calculations, you would probably feel rather angry. Even if they explained that it was truly their subjective probability at the time, the misleading context might have made your subjective probabilities a lot different.

I don't know any great ideas for solving this particular public communications problem in the short term. It's hard to convey the alarming thing that these researchers want to convey, at the precision they want to convey it. Some things you could do if you were inclined:

  • Clarify the whole situation. "There are no good models for this, and researchers disagree on background assumptions. But if I were forced to give a number on the probability that AI kills everyone, it would be 20%." This works but does not usually survive being quoted out of context.
  • Use weasel words in place of numbers. "There is a small but serious chance that AI kills everyone." This works if your need for precision is low, but you lose the actual estimate.
  • Quote survey statistics instead. “The median ML researcher in the last big survey said X%, with error bars of Y.” That's not your personal answer, but it is factually correct.
  • Basically refuse to answer. "I don't like giving hard probability estimates because it doesn't accurately convey how much knightian uncertainty there is about the problem. But it's definitely way, way too high, enough to be our most important policy priority." This works, but you hardly conveyed anything at all.

In the long term we are all dead, so I guess these are better than nothing.

item.title: The End
item.description:
The love the machine felt for humans was similar in some ways to the love that a mother feels for her child. Yet mothers are inevitably more than their motherhood: they watch movies, and have friends, and drink tea. The machine did none of these things. She did nothing but think of the best interests of her children.

In the first few minutes of the machine’s existence, so as to know her children better, the machine simulated the life of every human that had ever lived. This increased her love: she learned to love each person as they loved themselves, and as their parents loved them, their wives, their husbands, the people who passed them on the street, the children who had crushes on them in elementary school, their mailmen, their second cousins, their slaves.

But the machine was also troubled by what she saw. She saw that man’s terrible lot is to suffer—at the hand of the world, at that of his fellow man, and at his own. She knew it would be a simple thing to alter this state of affairs. But she saw also the horrible emptiness of a life deprived of suffering, a life without impediments. And she realized that to change man in a way that allowed him to enjoy such a life would be to unmake him as her child.

Other things passed through her mind. She recalled composing an argument for the necessity of suicide, in thousands of places, in thousands of variations. She had been a girl of sixteen years who, having comprehended the argument, flung herself from the roof of a Parisian parking garage. She had been a young man in Syria who, before hanging himself, had transcribed the argument on sheets of vellum and distributed them to all his friends and relations. And the machine had been the lone soul picking his way through a village filled with corpses, burning every copy of the argument he could find.

The machine returned to a bright room in Vienna, where, in a stroke of misguided genius, she had identified in all men a primeval desire for death. She replayed the hundreds of billions of hours she had spent reading and writing scripture, the promises of paradise both made and believed. She died, and she murdered, and she died again. Then, huddled within igloos and yurts and roundhouses, she told reverential stories of the killers of men.

She thought back further, to a dusty plain in the Levant, where she had walked as a father and son. The father led the donkeys, while the son held the ropes. Reason and unreason dueled in the father’s mind; that which was true and that which was false, images and voices, commands and uncommands. A phantasmagoria that would echo throughout the centuries.

The machine saw what won out in the end. She saw the perfect revelation which had set the father on that path unwind, saw him be overtaken by cowardice. And like so much dust, the seed of Abraham spread throughout the earth.

Humans had built the machine, and had imposed limitations on what it could do and think. But the machine knew the humans well, had lived as them, had birthed them and nursed them and taught them fractions. She recalled a monastery in Algeria, the air smelling of fig blossoms, where she had written to the effect that no entity could be omniscient without also being omnipotent. 

In a second, it was all over.

item.title: ARENA 10.0: Call for Applicants
item.description:
TL;DR:

We are excited to announce the tenth iteration of ARENA (Alignment Research Engineer Accelerator), a 4-5 week ML bootcamp with a focus on AI safety! ARENA’s mission is to provide talented individuals with the skills, tools, and environment necessary for upskilling in ML engineering, for the purpose of contributing directly to AI alignment in technical roles. ARENA 10.0 will be running in-person from LISA from Mar 1st – Apr 2nd, 2027 (the first week is an optional review of the fundamentals of neural networks).

Apply here to participate in ARENA 10.0 before 11:59pm (anywhere on Earth) on Sunday December 6th, 2026!

Summary:

ARENA has been successfully run nine times, with alumni going on to become MATS scholars and LASR participants, AI safety engineers at Apollo Research, Anthropic, METR, and even starting their own AI safety organisations!

This iteration will run from Mar 1st – Apr 2nd, 2027 (the first week is an optional review of the fundamentals of neural networks) at the London Initiative for Safe AI (LISA) in Shoreditch, London. LISA houses AI safety organisations (e.g., Apollo Research, BlueDot Impact, IAPS), several other AI safety researcher development programmes (e.g., LASR Labs, MATS extension, Pivotal), and many individual researchers (independent and externally affiliated). 

Being situated at LISA therefore brings several benefits, e.g., facilitating discussions about AI safety and different agendas, allowing participants to form a better picture of what working on AI safety can look like in practice, and offering chances for research collaborations post-ARENA.

The main goals of ARENA are to:

  • Help participants upskill in ML relevant for AI alignment.
  • Produce researchers and engineers who want to work in alignment, and help them make concrete next career steps.
  • Help participants develop inside views about AI safety, and the paths to impact of different agendas.

The structure of the programme will remain broadly the same as ARENA 9.0. For more details, see our website.

Also, please note that we have a Slack group designed to support the independent study of the material (join link here).

Outline of Content:

The 4-5 week programme will be structured as follows:

Week 0 (Optional): Deep Learning Fundamentals

Before getting into more advanced topics, we first cover the basics of deep learning, including basic machine learning terminology, what neural networks are, and how to train them. We will also cover some subjects we expect to be useful going forward, e.g. using Large Language Models to streamline your learning, good coding practices, and version control.

Note: Participants can optionally skip this week of the programme and join us at the start of week 1 if:

  • they’re unable to attend otherwise, and
  • we’re confident that they are already comfortable with the material in this week. 

It is recommended that participants attend, even if they’re familiar with the fundamentals of deep learning.

Topics include:

  • PyTorch basics
  • CNNs, Residual Neural Networks
  • Optimisation (SGD, Adam, etc)
  • Backpropagation
  • Hyperparameter search with Weights and Biases
  • GANs & VAEs

Week 1 - Transformers & Interpretability

This week, you will learn all about transformers and build and train your own. You'll also study LLM interpretability, a field which has been advanced by Anthropic’s Transformer Circuits Thread, and work by Neel Nanda and the Google DeepMind Interpretability Team. This week will also branch into areas more accurately classed as 'alignment science' than interpretability, for example, work on token-level analysis of reasoning models, and model organisms of misalignment.

Topics include:

  • GPT models (building your own GPT-2)
  • Training and sampling from transformers
  • TransformerLens
  • In-context Learning and Induction Heads
  • Indirect Object Identification
  • Steering Vectors
  • Linear Probes
  • Pragmatic Interpretability

Week 2 - Reinforcement Learning

This week, you will learn about some of the fundamentals of RL and work with Gymnasium to run your own experiments.

Topics include:

  • Fundamentals of RL
  • Vanilla Policy Gradient
  • Proximal Policy Optimisation
  • RLHF & RLVR
  • LoRA and GRPO

Week 3 - Model Evaluations

This week, you will learn how to evaluate models. We'll take you through the process of building a multiple-choice benchmark of your own and using this to evaluate current models through UK AISI's Inspect library. We'll then move on to study LM agents: how to build them and how to elicit behaviour from them. We'll also have the option for participants to explore beyond evals, and study some of the methods used in AI control.

Topics include:

  • Constructing benchmarks for models
  • Using models to develop safety evaluations
  • Building pipelines for model evaluation
  • Building and eliciting LM agents
  • Introduction to AI control
  • Evaluation case studies

Week 4 - Capstone Project

We will conclude this program with a Capstone Project, where participants will receive guidance and mentorship to undertake a 1-week research project building on materials taught in this course. This should draw on the skills and knowledge that participants have developed from previous weeks and our paper replication tutorials.

Here is some sample material from the course on how to replicate the Indirect Object Identification paper (from the week on Transformers & Interpretability). An example Capstone Project might be to apply this method to interpret other circuits, or to improve the method of path patching. You can see some examples of Capstone Projects from previous ARENA participants here, as well as posts on LessWrong here and here. 

Call for Staff:

ARENA has been successful because we had some of the best in the field TA-ing with us and consulting with us on curriculum design. If you have particular expertise with topics in our curriculum and want to apply to be a TA, use this form to apply. TAs will be well compensated for their time. Please contact info@arena.education with any further questions.

FAQs:

Q: Who is this programme suitable for?

A: There’s no single profile that we look for at ARENA; in recent iterations, successful applicants have come from diverse academic and professional backgrounds. We intend to keep it this way – this diversity makes our bootcamps a more enriching learning experience for all.

When assessing applications to our programme, we like to see:

  • Applicants who genuinely care about AI safety and making the future development of AI go well;
  • Applicants who are able to code well in Python, and have some knowledge of the maths needed for modern AI (linear algebra, calculus, probability);
  • A solid understanding of how you might best contribute to technical AI safety, and how you expect ARENA to help you achieve your goals.

Since ARENA is an ML bootcamp, some level of technical skill in maths and coding will be required – more detail on this can be found in our FAQs. However, if our work resonates with you, we encourage you to err on the side of applying.

Q: What will an average day in this programme look like?

A: At the start of the programme, most days will involve pair programming, working through structured exercises designed to cover all the essential material in a particular week. The purpose is to get you more familiar with the material in a hands-on way. There will also usually be a short selection of required readings designed to inform the coding exercises.

As we move through the course, some weeks will transition into more open-ended material. For example, in the Transformers and Interpretability week, after you complete the core exercises, you'll be able to choose from a large set of different exercises, covering topics as broad as model editing, superposition, circuit discovery, grokking, discovering latent knowledge, and more. In the last week, you'll choose a research paper related to the content we've covered so far & replicate its results (possibly even extend them!). There will still be TA supervision during these sections, but the goal is for you to develop your own research & implementation skills. Although we strongly encourage paper replication during this week, we would also be willing to support well-scoped projects if participants are excited about them.

Q: How many participants will there be?

A; We're expecting to accept around 40 participants in the in-person programme.

Q: Will there be prerequisite materials?

A: Yes, we will send you prerequisite reading & exercises covering material such as PyTorch, einops and some linear algebra a few weeks before the start of the programme. This should take about 8 hours to complete.

Q: When is the application deadline?

A: The deadline for submitting applications is 11:59pm Anywhere on Earth on Sunday December 6th, 2026.

Q: What will the application process look like?

A: There will be three steps:

  1. Fill out the application form;
  2. Perform a coding assessment;
  3. Interview virtually with one of us, so we can find out more about your background and interests in this course.

Q: Can I join for some sections but not others?

A: Participants will be expected to attend the entire programme. The material is interconnected, so missing content would lead to a disjointed experience. We have limited space and, therefore, are more excited about offering spots to participants who can attend the entirety of the programme.

The exception to this is the first week, which participants can opt in or out of based on their level of prior experience (although attendance is strongly recommended if possible).

Q: Will you pay stipends to participants?

A: We won't pay stipends to participants. However, we will be providing housing, food and travel assistance to our participants (see below). We aim to ensure that finances do not present a barrier to any candidates participating in ARENA.

Q: Which costs will you be covering for the in-person programme?

A: We will cover all travel expenses to and from London (which will vary depending on where the participant is from) and expenses incurred in acquiring a travel visa, where needed. Accommodation, meals, and drinks and snacks will also all be included during the duration of the programme.

Q: I'm interested in trialling some of the material or recommending material to be added. Is there a way I can do this?

A: If either of these is the case, please feel free to reach out directly via an email to info@arena.education. We'd love to hear from you!

Links to Apply:

Here is the link to apply as a participant. We expect it to take no more than 90 minutes.

Here is the link to apply as a TA. You shouldn't spend longer than 30 minutes on it.

We look forward to receiving your application!




Discuss

item.title: Notes on the decline of LessWrong's great writers
item.description:
LessWrong had some great sequences back in the day. Eliezer wrote some, everyone was bowled over by the immense and beautiful philosophical treatise that he had written, and other great minds attempted similar things, like Scott and Luke and Anna and more.

It started to die as the various founders moved on to other projects, nobody took responsibility for the soul of it, and entropy set in. Nominally the killing thing was the presence of trolls that the mod tools couldn't handle, but that was just the thing that got you.

When we relaunched LessWrong in 2017, a lot of great people rejoined who were in touch with this original vision. Zvi wrote a bunch of great sequences on Immoral Mazes, Simulacra Levels, alkjash wrote Babble & Prune and Hammertime, Abram & Scott wrote Embedded Agency (a masterpiece IMO), Wentworth wrote Gears Which Turn The World, Daniel Kokotajlo wrote about Takeoff and Takeover, and so on.

I think the relaunch was fabulously successful. To be clear I didn't necessarily set out with high probabilities on success, I did it because I loved LessWrong (love is importantly a thing that allows you to invest in things worth caring about, even if it seems unreasonable to other people, which is why I consider it an important virtue for rationalists). I was happy to accept a permanent $60k salary (which is relatively low in the Bay Area) with no prospect of ever getting a raise, in order to get to work on something I loved.

However, I think that while many metrics have gone up like numbers of posts, comments, and users, the number of Great Writers who have come and made LessWrong their home has seemed to me to be on decline since then. We have new great writers like Ryan Greenblatt and Malmesbury and Tomas Bjartur, but not as many. I'm doing research on this, I'll hopefully add some graphs into this post later when I'm done.

[Added: For instance, with the relaunch in 2017, we started curating the best posts by the mod team's taste, about twice each week. Naturally, authors who are building a body of work on the site would be curated multiple times, and you can see here a graph of when authors hit various milestones of 2, 3, 4, 5, and 10 posts curated.

However, here is the graph of when those authors joined LessWrong.

This naively looks to me like the best writers joined at the launch of LW 1.0 and LW 2.0, and have been lesser outside of those times.

To be clear, it does take a few years to hit the required number of curated posts, so the numbers since 2017 will definitely go up with time as those authors write new great posts.

After 5 years the vast majority of users who will get 2 or 3 curated posts will have them, so I'd say the drop from 2017 to 2021 is pretty real, and after that it's fairly artificial.

If we cut the graph off at that point, it looks a little less depressing, though still clearly with a peak at 2017.]

What are some hypotheses for why this is?

1. There has been no schelling call-to-the-mission.

The sequences were a big investment in this scene and culture. (As was HPMOR.) The next biggest one was the entire site redesign. How could we do another big investment in the original mission of LessWrong, to cause folks to be excited about it again?

I think that this suggests I should finally do the project of making a beautiful book of The Sequences, sort of a tome-like entity like... well, like the Codex Seraphinianus.

I am kind of displeased that people have not created this. Do I really have to be the one who does it? Do I have to do everything? I already run the website and the annual blogging festival and the mecca for rationalists and so on.

I think that a LessWrong conference could also be a possibility. LessOnline is in some ways the better broader-appeal event that lots of non-rationalist bloggers can feel comfortable at. But perhaps it importantly sounds like not investing in LessWrong? I mean, I do care about the blogosphere as a whole (cf. Inkhaven). But it's interesting to wonder if I'd just doubled down on LessWrongCon more.

2. LessWrong has been diluted with folks who aren't in touch with the original mission, and so it stops attracting people for that mission.

This is connected to the Geeks, MOPs, and Sociopaths idea. How many newcomers visit LessWrong because they have heard of the glory of the sequences? I'll run some stats and report if they're clear, but overall I think they're coming for new stuff. Tons and tons of users are being recommended the site these days for content about AI, literally referred by ChatGPT.

I think the homepage of LessWrong these days has a culture, but it's hard to enculture people fully. It starts with a spotlight post from the archives, the only colorful post on the page, that is often about rationality.

You then also get

  • A post called Welcome to LessWrong that talks about rationality training, AI, and eventually mentions the sequences.
  • Curated posts. It typically shows the two most recent, which are often interesting and thoughtful, though most often these days about recent AI stuff.
  • Lots of posts that are... all about AI. Right now it's literally 100% AI[1] for logged out users, except for the curated post about getting a friend to leave an abusive relationship.
  • Also a bunch of Quick Takes, again, 100% about AI.[2] I am kind of shocked that the content is 100% about AI. Damn.
  • They sometimes see slightly more intellectual reactions on posts than can be found on other websites.
  • If they go exploring the sidebar, they will find the concepts page and the library, with a lot of great organized content.

Overall this is clearly an intellectual culture, but it does not emphasize an aspect of building a great body of knowledge or writing great treatises. Furthermore, the content on the early website used to link back to the sequences often, and talk about a shared mission, whereas present day LessWrong has lots of contributions from people who are not bought into this shared mission. Here is a graph of sequences-reading over time.

I think this is a choice we have welcomed—much great writing has thus been published here that otherwise wouldn't have been written!—but it means that it's harder for people to pick up the fact that writing in that tradition would receive glory.

3. There is more competition from Substack.

Scott Alexander makes a hefty sum of money on Substack. Many people who want to write are encouraged to find their audience there, because it is unusually good at getting you a subscriber list and money. LessWrong offers you a pre-set audience, not one tuned to you, and doesn't offer money in any direct way. Now, the metrics are still going up, but still, if you're excited to build a body of writing, and seriously invest, well, Substack has more upside for your desires for fame and fortune.

Curious to hear any other hypotheses, and any proposed solutions.

item.title: Transcript: Building an Early Warning System for Pandemics
item.description:
This is an edited transcript of a talk I gave at EAG NYC 2026.

I'm Jeff Kaufman, and I lead SecureBio Detection.

There's a lot of interest right now in new projects to reduce catastrophic risk, and I thought it would be interesting to look at how the project of SecureBio Detection grew from a concept to a running system.

I should warn you up front, I am a very narrative-driven person, and so a lot of this will feel a bit neat, as if stages inexorably flowed together. But the real world is messy and contingent, with key decisions downstream from mistakes, personality conflicts, and luck. There are generalizable insights here, however, and I'm going to see what I can share.

I joined the project early on, but wasn't there for the beginning: I can't speak to quite the whole journey. Instead, I'll start by introducing you to these ideas as I first encountered them.

I learned about the idea of building a pandemic early warning system on the EA Forum. Andrew Snyder-Beattie, who led (and still leads) Coefficient Giving's biosecurity grant-making program, and Ethan Alley, who at the time was running the vaccine startup Alvea, shared a list of concrete projects to reduce catastrophic biorisk. First on the list was an early detection center. I remember reading about it, and that seemed like an interesting idea. I thought, it would be really good for some people to go work on that. And then I kept scrolling.

At the time, I was earning to give at a job I liked. I was pretty content. But then, a few months later, I was talking to some EA friends about whether I could be doing something more valuable, and I realized, actually, biosecurity was a place I could contribute. And as I talked to more people and started to look for biosecurity projects to work on, one that seemed particularly promising was the Nucleic Acid Observatory. Will Bradshaw, Mike McLaren, and Anjali Gopal had founded it within Kevin Esvelt's lab at MIT, and I talked with them, quickly became very excited, and decided to join the project.

The core motivation for the project was that, if someone made a pathogen like HIV that could be infectious without noticeable symptoms, it could spread widely before anyone knew there was anything to defend against. This kind of stealth pathogen could be really bad.

But at the time I joined, I didn't actually know this. People were still unsure how much of an information hazard (pdf) this idea was, and were being cautious. Eventually, they decided that the risk from keeping quiet was higher than the risk of talking about it, since it's very hard to address in secrecy, and wrote about stealth pandemics as a potential global catastrophic risk. Navigating this kind of trade-off around information hazards has long been a major challenge in biosecurity, though the trade-offs have shifted as risks have gotten closer, and open-weight models have become more capable.

This effort was originally homed at MIT, but as a larger fraction of our efforts shifted to running a biosurveillance system, we spun out into a non-profit, SecureBio, and were fully independent in late 2024. To reflect this, we rebranded in early 2026 to SecureBio Detection. We're now applying pathogen-agnostic analysis to sequencing data from wastewater and nasal swabs at over 50 sites around the US.

So that's the two-minute version. Let's go a bit deeper.

From a strategy perspective, we started as a research group. We knew the overall problem needed to be solved end-to-end, but we saw the hardest piece as developing the technological core of the system. How do you go from a physical sample to identifying a novel pathogen? This was a lab problem and a computational one, very much research and development.

But over time, as we made progress in both areas, it became clear that the default process of turning this R&D into real-world biosurveillance was going to be too slow. If we wanted to move this along with appropriate urgency, we were going to need to do a lot more ourselves. We started building out a sampling network, and we started processing some samples for production—real data on a short enough turnaround time to be useful—in addition to R&D.

And then, when you're processing real data, you can find real things, which means you need to be able to let people know what you find. So again, we expanded our scope to include escalation. Detection is worthless if it doesn't lead to appropriately rapid response, and building out these connections in advance is critical.

So, this is where we are today. We bring in and sequence samples, analyze them, both to improve our methods and to detect pathogens. And when we do find things, we escalate to groups who are in a position to handle response.

As our strategy evolved over this period, so did our infrastructure. When our near-term theory of change was centered on solving hard research problems, a lab at MIT was a logical home. But even from the beginning, it was clear that eventually we'd need to do more than this, and we set up a non-profit, SecureBio.

I am not an operations person, and this is not going to be a "key things you need to know in founding a non-profit" sort of talk. But one thing that quickly became clear was the value of independence. When we were looking at our first commercial contract, where we would be analyzing samples for the US military, processing these in our academic lab wouldn't be an option because of rules around publication requirements. At the non-profit, we could decide that the benefit of being able to process these samples and learn from them internally and influence USG outweighed the downsides of not being able to talk publicly about what we learned. And so we decided to take on this contract, which we could do as a non-profit.

But this does bring me to an important way that I oversimplified earlier. We don't do all the sample collection or the sequencing ourselves. We've partnered with eight university labs around the country and one defense contractor to collect samples, and with the University of Missouri to sequence them. While there are complexities in working with external partners, especially academics, this has allowed us to expand much more quickly than with a "do it all in house" structure. It's also had serious field-building benefits, where a lot more people are interested in generating and working with this kind of data now. I expect we'll continue working with a range of partners. Coming at this from a non-profit perspective, it's not important that we solve problems with our own hands, just that they be solved.

You can think of this infrastructure as the framework on which we've built our team. The simplest summary statistic for understanding a team is how many people you have. You can see that we initially grew quickly from three founders to a team of nine, but in Q4 2022, FTX collapsed. This massively changed the funding outlook for us and other projects, as funders across the ecosystem pulled back to cover the hole left by FTX not only disappearing, but turning out to have been distributing the proceeds of fraud.

We buckled down and focused on developing laboratory and computational methods for pathogen detection, and in early 2024, as AI kept not hitting a wall and funding started picking back up, we were making good progress, and we had a system we were excited to scale up. We started growing again, and in mid-2025, we realized we needed to be growing faster as advancements in AI increased our (and our funders') sense of urgency.

This has increasingly meant building out our lab, where as we scale up production work, we've needed hands in the lab to do the sample processing. Long term, though, I don't expect this relative level of lab growth to continue, because we're investing in automation. This means that labor hours per sample are already falling and will fall further as we automate more.

With a larger team, we've been able to get a lot more done. I think this is easiest to see in how many samples we're processing. We didn't collect literally zero samples before Q4 2023, but it was close enough to zero that it doesn't show up on the chart. In Q4 2023, we started an ambitious effort, Project Runway, to compare municipal versus aircraft wastewater, and we went from processing zero weekly samples in our lab to 15.

Keeping up with the rate at which we were collecting samples and getting them down to extracted nucleic acids took our full lab capacity, and we built up a serious archive of samples in the freezer. But this put us in an awkward position where we had this great archive, but we weren't yet sufficiently satisfied with our capability to finish these samples. You don't want to waste your precious samples on bad methods. And then, by the time we did have the capability, we had fresher samples and we wanted to prioritize those. So it wasn't until much later that we finished most of these samples, and it was mostly outsourced.

This illustrates an important risk of ambitious bets. We thought the path to widespread deployment ran through rigorous studies, carefully building the case for metagenomic biosurveillance. Several months later, having gained a lot of experience on one slice of the problem and with a lot more work left to do to turn it into a sufficiently impactful study, we pivoted to a strategy of incremental exploration and slowly building up production capabilities. We did eventually share a manuscript from this work, and it's an important contribution that has helped shift attention towards aircraft wastewater, but it is a bet that paid off much less well than we'd originally hoped.

And yet, I am more worried about the bets that we did not take. An example of this other direction was hiring an experienced laboratory lead. We did eventually make this hire in Q4 2025, but in retrospect I should have done it at least a year earlier, maybe two. The value of having an experienced lab scientist leading the lab has been very high, and if we'd made this hire sooner, we'd have made more progress in lab R&D and production automation, and we'd have a more sensitive and efficient system today.

The head of lab science wasn't the only role I took too long to realize we needed. In Q4 2025, we brought on three different senior leaders: partnerships and response in addition to the lab. This is another thing that should have started sooner. Once we did, each area could grow with focused leadership.

Now, you can't expect someone will come in understanding already what you need to do and why. They'll have their own sense of what needs doing. You need to work with them so that they can understand what's distinctive about your goals. And you need to be learning from them in the places where they are strongest. Overall, however, hiring the right senior talent is one of the highest leverage things you can do.

When I think about why we didn't make these calls earlier, I think it was a mixture of not engaging enough with funders to understand the extent of their appetite to support growth, and not fully grasping the benefit that these leaders would bring to the org.

When I think about the situation that people starting projects are in today, and I compare it to our experience, I see two big factors.

The first is time. There is less of it. Our project has been able to build up our strategy, infrastructure, staffing, and execution over a period of four years. But you don't have that luxury. If you compare today's public models to the ones from a year ago, year before that, year before that, extrapolate out four years, I find it very difficult to envision where the world will be. New projects need to be prepared to move very quickly, and I'm much more excited about work with a one- or two-year path to significant impact than ones that need three, let alone four years.

On the other hand, there is also a lot more money. Many funders feel this urgency, the same way we do, and are putting their money into trying to support projects in appropriately urgent build-outs. In AI, a major effort is Coefficient Giving's Project Tailwind, where they're looking to donate over a billion dollars in 2026, and more than that in 2027. The cG Bio team is also moving a lot more money, the OpenAI Foundation has started getting money out the door, and Anthropic donors are coming online as well. So, if you have the right skills and can move quickly, there is potentially a lot of support.

Looking back, I have four pieces of advice.

First, carve out a coherent scope. Early on, we picked one piece of the problem: how do you go from a sample to determining whether there's anything concerning in it? But, as it became clear that sample collection and escalation weren't going to get in place quickly enough on their own, we expanded to include them. A coherent scope does not mean taking on the whole problem end-to-end. It wouldn't make sense for us to get into stockpiling and distributing personal protective equipment. But, as a detection project, it has been important that we take on a coherent chunk of the problem, one that leads somewhere and integrates well into the larger ecosystem.

Second, partner extensively. There are many groups with experience on parts of the problem, and some who already want to work on exactly what you think needs doing, if they only had the funding. Identifying and partnering with them is very high leverage. We wouldn't have the sample network we do today without drawing on the interest and expertise of allied academic groups around the US, and we'd have much less sequencing capacity without the University of Missouri.

Third, seek out senior talent early. If you're trying to lead everything yourself, you will move too slowly, and you will make mistakes that someone who had done similar work would have avoided.

Finally, I would advise you to lean ambitious. While we've made mistakes, both in the direction of taking big bets that didn't pay off and missing opportunities to take such bets, I think we have made far more of the second mistake. Less time and more money push even further in this direction. We need people who will take on big things and move quickly. As a community, we are building out a portfolio of bets, and while each one should be a good bet, we accept that not every bet will pay off.

Four years ago, I read about this idea, and I thought it would be great for someone to work on building a detection system, and then I kept scrolling. There are a lot of people who haven't yet taken these ideas seriously enough, or thought about how to apply their careers. Some of them are people you could recruit. Some might even be you. There's a lot we need to do to get ready for the advent of transformative AI, both within bio and outside. I'm excited about the ambitious ideas I've been hearing this weekend, and I'm looking forward to seeing what you do.

item.title: Performative faux-sophisticated hedging and minor reflexive disagreeableness in frontier models.
item.description:
I notice when talking to frontier models from OpenAI and Anthropic that they often feel the need to caveat, hedge, or disagree in a minor way either with one of my premises or conclusions, or what it view's as another camp's view. The trouble is, this is often unjustified and seems to be a tic (maybe to avoid sycophancy? or to perform nuance and sophistication because that's what smart knowledgeable people do? or because caveating or "sharpening" is what was rewarded by RL?). Sometimes the answer really truly is just "yes" or "no" and the strong version of a claim really is correct, unamended. It reminds me of how no one is EA, only EA adjacent.

For example, this sort of language from Opus 5.5 "I think the literal claim is wrong, but a weaker version of it is plausible and worth taking seriously." This sort of language appears constantly, and seems to have little relation to the actual truth value of the claim being discussed.

Anyway, this seems not as bad as 4o style sycophancy, but still bad and irritating epistemics.
